newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Conf. Board sees dlr/mark at 1.75 in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Conf. Board sees dlr/mark at 1.75 in 1997.

text.p: The dollar will rise to 1.75 marks by the end of 1997, possibly advancing as high as 1.85 to 2.00 marks in 1998, according to the latest Conference Board forecast.
But because dollar/yen has already risen sharply over the last two years, its upside is limited to 125 in second-quarter 1997 and 130 through 1998, the forecasting group said.
The dollar ended at 124.60 yen and 1.6978 marks Wednesday.
Strong U.S. economic fundamentals relative to Europe and Japan will continue to draw huge investment flows into U.S. securities and the dollar, the group said in a release.
Dollar-buying has also increased as European nations have begun taking difficult economic steps toward a single currency, the proposed euro, by the 1999 target date, the group said in a release.
The forecast "calls for the deutschemark to fall to 1.75 by the end of 1997 and even further in 1998 because of the turmoil surrounding the lauch of the euro," the release said.
The dollar typically becomes substantially overvalued before it corrects lower, meaning the U.S. currency has considerable room to rise before topping out, the board said.

"Because the extent of dollar strength over the next two years is likely to be greater than at any time since the early 1980s, it would be useful to test scenarios with a 130-yen and 2.00-mark dollar," said Gail Fosler, senior vice president and chief economist at the Conference Board.
The group cited "the strong relative performance of the U.S. economy, coupled with high U.S. real interest rates, relative to Japan and Germany," for the robust dollar outlook.
The growth of dollar-based global trade, boosted by rising oil prices, and the dollar's appeal as an alternative to the euro, bolster the dollar, the group added.
In fact European nations have ample reason to promote a strong dollar, or a weak mark, said Fosler.

"A weak mark relieves Europe of the interest rate and competitive pressures that have held down growth and raised European budget deficits, thus helping a broad base of European countries meet the (single-currency) criteria," Fosler said.
"Indeed, a weak mark may be a necessary precondition to achieving monetary union. In sum, we are entering a dollar-dominated world without clear currency alternatives."
